rv.q: Like Boleyn, Anna captivates powerful men; but also like Boleyn, she learns how quickly patriarchal authority can turn vicious.
Pickett’s play is a tour de force, and 1536 one of those theatrical moments that stays with you for a very long time.
The representation of what it is like to move as a woman in a patriarchal society – whether in 1536 or 2025 – was absolutely brilliant.
Tense and original, with a creeping dread, it comes across as a first-rate thriller and a top comedy too.
It's a bold, idiosyncratic and disturbingly funny work that slightly overplays its hand towards the end.
What you actually get is the kind of simplistic, feminist-lite drama about the evils of patriarchy that you normally encounter in a one-hour slot at the Edinburgh Fringe.
The result is one of the sharpest, funniest and most unsettling pieces of new writing currently on the London stage.
It’s a bold, essential piece of theatre that the West End should always look to have on its stages.
This is a play that we have been crying out for - and a true testament to what theatre can do.
One of the great joys of theatre is that sometimes you're in the room when an extraordinary voice breaks through, when something really quite special happens.
Exceptionally well-acted and taut, 1536 is a thought-provoking and emotionally engrossing experience.
This is a provocative and accomplished work that marks Pickett as a distinctive new voice in British theatre.
1536 is a foul-mouthed, furious, frenetically funny ride through the lives of three young women living in Henry VIII’s England.

cn.t: Pickett's acclaimed debut uses Anne Boleyn's fall to explore misogyny through three Essex women in this foul-mouthed, darkly funny zeitgeist hit, though one critic dismisses it as simplistic feminist-lite drama.
